title: Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task (`setIfAbsent` with TTL).
shortTitle: Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task
topicTitle: Write Redis-based distributed lock logic for a scheduled task

s1_definition.profdef: A Redis distributed lock lets multiple instances of a service agree that only one of them runs a critical section at a time. It is implemented with an atomic `SET key value NX PX ttl` (exposed in Spring as `opsForValue().setIfAbsent(key, token, ttl)`), which succeeds only if the key does not already exist and auto-expires after the TTL so a crashed holder never deadlocks the system. The lock value is a unique token so that only the owner can release it, and release is done with a Lua script that checks the token before deleting, making check-and-delete atomic. For scheduled tasks across a horizontally scaled deployment, this guarantees the job fires once per schedule, not once per instance.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs the nightly interest calculation. The service runs on five servers for high availability, so at 2 AM all five wake up and all five try to calculate interest for Rajesh and Priya, which would credit interest five times. To prevent that, there is a single key hanging on a hook in a shared room (Redis). The rule: whoever grabs the key first does the job, and everyone else sees the hook is empty and quietly goes back to sleep. The key is tagged with the name of who took it, so only that person can return it. And the key automatically falls back on the hook after a set time, so if the holder faints mid-job, the key is not lost forever.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use SET NX PX (setIfAbsent with TTL) so only one instance acquires the lock, the TTL prevents deadlock on crash, and a token-checked Lua release ensures only the owner unlocks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Redis distributed lock lets multiple instances of a service agree that only one of them runs a critical section at a time. It is implemented with an atomic `SET key value NX PX ttl` (exposed in Spring as `opsForValue().setIfAbsent(key, token, ttl)`), which succeeds only if the key does not already exist and auto-expires after the TTL so a crashed holder never deadlocks the system. The lock value is a unique token so that only the owner can release it, and release is done with a Lua script that checks the token before deleting, making check-and-delete atomic. For scheduled tasks across a horizontally scaled deployment, this guarantees the job fires once per schedule, not once per instance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs the nightly interest calculation. The service runs on five servers for high availability, so at 2 AM all five wake up and all five try to calculate interest for Rajesh and Priya, which would credit interest five times. To prevent that, there is a single key hanging on a hook in a shared room (Redis). The rule: whoever grabs the key first does the job, and everyone else sees the hook is empty and quietly goes back to sleep. The key is tagged with the name of who took it, so only that person can return it. And the key automatically falls back on the hook after a set time, so if the holder faints mid-job, the key is not lost forever.

**One line to remember:** Use SET NX PX (setIfAbsent with TTL) so only one instance acquires the lock, the TTL prevents deadlock on crash, and a token-checked Lua release ensures only the owner unlocks.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem it solves. When you scale a service horizontally for availability, every instance has the same scheduled job. Without coordination, a cron at 2 AM fires on all five instances and the interest posting runs five times. You need mutual exclusion across machines, which a local Java lock cannot provide because each JVM has its own lock object. Redis, being a single shared fast store, becomes the coordination point.

Why setIfAbsent with TTL. The core operation is Redis `SET key value NX PX milliseconds`. NX means "only set if the key does not already exist," which is atomic, so exactly one of the racing instances wins. PX sets an expiry in milliseconds. In Spring Data Redis this is `redisTemplate.opsForValue().setIfAbsent("lock:interest-posting", token, Duration.ofSeconds(60))`, which returns true to the one winner and false to everyone else. The winner runs the job; the losers skip.

Why a TTL is mandatory. Suppose the winner acquires the lock and then its JVM crashes or the machine dies before releasing. Without a TTL the lock key stays forever and the job never runs again on any instance, a permanent deadlock. The TTL is a safety valve: the lock auto-expires, so the next scheduled run can acquire it. You set the TTL comfortably longer than the worst-case job duration so the lock does not expire while the job is still running.

Why a unique token. The lock value must be a unique identifier for this acquisition, such as a UUID or instance-id plus timestamp. This prevents the classic wrong-release bug: instance A acquires the lock, the job runs long and the TTL expires, Redis frees the lock, instance B acquires it, and then instance A finishes and blindly deletes the lock, but it just deleted B's lock. By storing a unique token and releasing only if the stored token equals mine, A sees the token no longer matches and does not delete B's lock.

Why release must be atomic with a Lua script. Releasing naively is "GET the key, if it equals my token then DEL it." But between the GET and the DEL, the TTL could expire and another instance could acquire, so you would delete their lock. Redis solves this by running a small Lua script atomically on the server: `if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`. The check and delete happen as one indivisible operation, so you only ever delete your own lock.

Handling long-running jobs with a watchdog. If a job might run longer than the TTL, you either set a generous TTL or run a background watchdog that periodically extends the TTL (also via a token-checked Lua script that calls PEXPIRE only if the token matches) while the job is still alive. This is what libraries like Redisson do automatically with lock leases.

When to use a library versus hand-rolling. For a simple scheduled-task guard, hand-rolled setIfAbsent plus Lua release is perfectly fine and easy to reason about. For stronger guarantees across Redis failover you can use Redisson, which implements the Redlock algorithm, lock leasing, watchdog renewal, and reentrancy. The senior nuance is honesty about guarantees: a single-Redis lock is not a perfect distributed lock under network partitions and failover; it is a practical "mostly once" guard that, combined with an idempotent job, is correct in practice. For money-critical jobs you also make the job itself idempotent so that even a rare double-run does not double-post.

The combination to remember is lock plus idempotency. The lock makes double execution rare; idempotency makes it harmless if it ever happens.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India posts daily interest to savings accounts. The posting service runs on multiple instances for high availability, and a scheduled job fires every night.

Problem 1 — interest was posted multiple times. All three instances fired the job at 2 AM and each credited Rajesh's savings account, tripling his interest. This is why we need a distributed lock so only one instance actually runs the posting.

Problem 2 — one night a lock was taken and the instance crashed, and the job never ran again. The lock key was stuck with no expiry. This is why the lock must have a TTL that auto-expires, so the next night can acquire it.

Problem 3 — a long run expired its own lock and a second instance started, then the first instance finished and deleted the second's lock. This is why the lock value is a unique token and release is a token-checked atomic Lua script, so an instance only ever releases its own lock.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the lock logic: a `DistributedLock` abstraction with acquire (setIfAbsent with TTL and unique token) and release (token-checked atomic delete), a simulated `FakeRedis` that is thread-safe, and an `InterestPostingJob` guarded by the lock. Three threads simulate three instances racing to run the nightly job; only one succeeds, and the job is also idempotent as a safety net.

redis-cli
> SET lock:interest-posting my-token NX PX 120000

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three instances fire the nightly job at the same instant. Rajesh starts at 1,000,000 and Priya at 250,000.

Step 1: All three threads reach runNightly and call tryAcquire almost simultaneously. Each generates its own unique token.

Step 2: Each calls setIfAbsent on the same key. FakeRedis is synchronized, so the calls serialize. The first thread finds the key absent and sets it with its token and a 120-second TTL, returning true. The other two find the key present and not expired, so NX fails and they get false.

Step 3: Instance-2 (say the winner) gets a non-null token and logs ACQUIRED. Instances 1 and 3 get null and log that they skipped. Only one instance will post interest.

Step 4: The winner iterates accounts. Rajesh's daily interest is 1,000,000 times the daily rate, rounded to 109.60, credited once. Priya's is credited once. Balances update exactly once.

Step 5: In the finally block the winner calls release with its token. compareAndDelete finds the stored token equals the winner's token and deletes the key. If the losers had somehow called release, their token would not match and nothing would be deleted, protecting the owner's lock.

Step 6: Because the TTL also exists, even if the winner had crashed before releasing, the key would expire after 120 seconds and the next scheduled run could acquire it. No permanent deadlock.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-2 ACQUIRED lock — posting interest
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-1 did NOT get the lock — skipping (another instance is posting)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-3 did NOT get the lock — skipping (another instance is posting)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-2 credited 109.60 to SAV2001 (Rajesh Kumar), new balance 1000109.60
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] instance-2 credited 27.40 to CUR3001 (Priya Sharma), new balance 250027.40
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] FINAL Rajesh balance = 1000109.60
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] FINAL Priya balance  = 250027.40
```

Note the interest was credited exactly once, not three times.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  2 AM cron fires on ALL instances simultaneously
    │
    ├─ instance-1 ─┐
    ├─ instance-2 ─┼─ tryAcquire() → SET lock:interest-posting <token> NX PX 120000
    └─ instance-3 ─┘
                    │  (Redis serializes; NX = only-if-absent)
         ┌──────────┴──────────────┐
         ▼                         ▼
   WINNER (instance-2)        LOSERS (1 and 3)
   token = abc-123            setIfAbsent → false
         │                         │
         ▼                         ▼
   post interest ONCE         skip (log + return)
   Rajesh +109.60
   Priya  +27.40
         │
         ▼
   release(abc-123) → Lua: get==token ? del : 0  → deletes OWN lock only
         │
         ▼
   (safety) if winner crashed → TTL expires in 120s → next run acquires
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Redis distributed lock lets me guarantee that a scheduled job runs once per schedule rather than once per instance, which matters the moment I scale a service horizontally for availability, because then the same cron fires on every instance. On my project at National Bank of India the nightly interest posting ran on three instances, and without coordination all three credited Rajesh and Priya, tripling their interest. A local Java lock cannot fix this because each JVM has its own lock object, so I need a shared coordination point, and Redis is a fast single store that serves that role perfectly.

The core of the lock is the atomic SET key value NX PX operation, which in Spring Data Redis is opsForValue().setIfAbsent with a TTL. NX means set only if the key does not already exist, so when all three instances race, Redis guarantees exactly one wins and gets true while the others get false, and only the winner runs the job. The TTL is mandatory for safety: if the winner crashes after acquiring but before releasing, without a TTL the lock would stay forever and the job would never run again, a permanent deadlock, so the TTL auto-expires the lock and lets the next scheduled run acquire it. I set the TTL comfortably longer than the worst-case job duration.

Two subtle correctness points matter. First, the lock value must be a unique token like a UUID, not a constant, because of the wrong-release bug: if instance A's job runs past the TTL, Redis frees the lock, instance B acquires it, and then A finishes and blindly deletes the lock, it would delete B's lock. By storing a unique token and releasing only when the stored token still equals mine, A sees the mismatch and leaves B's lock alone. Second, the release must be atomic, so I use a small Lua script that reads the value and deletes it only if it equals my token in a single indivisible server-side operation, because a naive GET-then-DEL has a race between the two steps. For jobs that might outlast the TTL I either set a generous TTL or run a watchdog that extends it, which is what Redisson does automatically.

I am also honest about the guarantees. A single-Redis lock is a practical mostly-once guard, not a perfect distributed lock under network partitions and Redis failover, so for money-critical jobs I combine the lock with an idempotent job, for example a posting-date marker so that even a rare double-run does not double-post interest. The lock makes double execution rare and idempotency makes it harmless if it ever happens, and together they are correct in practice.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I acquire with setIfAbsent using NX plus a TTL so exactly one instance wins and a crash cannot deadlock, I store a unique token and release it with a token-checked atomic Lua script so I only ever unlock my own lock, and I back the lock with an idempotent job so the scheduled task is effectively run-once even across a horizontally scaled, highly available deployment.
